[[File:Withania somnifera00.jpg|thumb|Flower]]

'''''Withania somnifera''''', known commonly as '''ashwagandha''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 2011-10-29 }}</ref><ref name="drugs">{{cite web |title=Ashwagandha |url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/ashwagandha.html |publisher=Drugs.com |access-date=26 January 2026|date=3 December 2025}}</ref> is an [[evergreen]] shrub in the [[Solanaceae]] family that is native to the [[Middle East and North Africa]], other African regions, southern Europe, [[Indian subcontinent]], and [[Southeast Asia]].<ref name=kew/><ref name= GRIN/> Several other species in the genus ''[[Withania]]'' are morphologically similar.<ref name= drugs/> Other common names include '''Indian ginseng''' and '''winter cherry'''.<ref name=kew/><ref name= drugs/> 

''Withania somnifera'' is a short shrub {{cvt|35|–|75|cm}} tall with [[Trichome|tomentose]] branches, dull green [[Ellipse|elliptic]] leaves up to {{cvt|10|–|12|cm}} long, small green bell-shaped flowers, and orange-red ripe fruit. It is affected by various pests and diseases in India, which can damage [[plant health]] and reduce its [[secondary metabolite]] content.

The plant, particularly its root powder, has been used for centuries in [[Ayurveda|traditional Indian medicine]].<ref>{{Cite news |vauthors= Pasricha T|date=2024-03-02 |title= Advice {{!}} Should I take ashwagandha for sleep? Here's what the science says. |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wellness/2024/03/04/should-i-take-ashwagandha-benefits-risks/ |access-date=2024-03-07 |newspaper= [[The Washington Post]] |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> ''W. somnifera'' is commonly sold as a [[dietary supplement]] containing root or leaf powder or [[extract]]s.<ref name=drugs/><ref name="NIH">{{cite web|publisher=Office of Dietary Supplements, National Institutes of Health | place= US |date=2 May 2025|title= Ashwagandha - Health Professional Fact Sheet|access-date=19 May 2025|url= https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Ashwagandha-HealthProfessional/}}</ref> It is undergoing research for potential effects on stress, anxiety, and sleep, but current [[Evidence-based medicine|clinical evidence]] is insufficient to confirm its safety or efficacy.<ref name=drugs/><ref name=NIH/><ref name= hepa>{{cite journal |vauthors=Philips CA, Theruvath AH |title=A comprehensive review on the hepatotoxicity of herbs used in the Indian (Ayush) systems of alternative medicine |journal=Medicine (Baltimore) |volume=103 |issue=16 |article-number=e37903 |date=April 2024 |pmid=38640296 |pmc=11029936 |doi=10.1097/MD.0000000000037903 |type=Review}}</ref><ref name="opss">{{cite web |title= Ashwagandha in Dietary Supplement Products|publisher= Operation Supplement Safety, US Uniformed Services University |date=30 May 2025 |url=https://www.opss.org/article/ashwagandha-dietary-supplement-products |access-date=26 January 2026}}</ref> The primary [[Phytochemical|phytochemicals]] in ''W. somnifera'' are [[Withanolide|withanolides]]—structurally similar to [[Ginsenoside|ginsenosides]] in ''[[Panax ginseng]]''—along with [[Alkaloid|alkaloids]] and sitoindosides, leading to its nickname, Indian ginseng.

''Withania somnifera'' is generally well tolerated for up to about three months with mostly mild [[Side effect|side effects.]]<ref name="NIH" /> It should be avoided during pregnancy or in people with hormone-sensitive conditions.<ref name=drugs/><ref name=NIH/><ref name=hepa/> It has been linked to rare cases of [[liver injury]], particularly in people with preexisting liver conditions.<ref name= hepa/><ref name= "livertox">{{cite web |title=Ashwagandha |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548536/ |publisher= LiverTox, National Library of Medicine, US National Institutes of Health |date=3 December 2024 |access-date= 2025-05-19}}</ref>

==Description==
This species is a short shrub growing {{convert|35-75|cm|abbr=on}} tall. [[Tomentose]] branches extend radially from a central stem. Leaves are dull green, elliptic, and usually up to {{convert|10|–|12|cm|abbr=on}} long. The flowers are small, green, and bell-shaped. The ripe fruit is orange-red.<ref name=drugs/>

==Etymology==
The Latin species name {{lang|la|somnifera}} means "sleep-inducing".<ref>{{cite book | author = Stearn, W. T. | year = 1995 | title = Botanical Latin: History, Grammar, Syntax, Terminology and Vocabulary | edition = 4th | publisher = Timber Press | isbn = 978-0-88192-321-6 | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/botanicallatin00will }}</ref> The name ''ashwagandha'' is a combination of the [[Sanskrit]] words ''{{transliteration|sa|ashva}}'', meaning "horse", and ''{{transliteration|sa|gandha}}'', meaning "smell", reflecting that the root has a strong, horse-like odor.<ref name=drugs/>

==Cultivation==
''Withania somnifera'' is cultivated in many of the drier regions of [[India]]. It is also found in [[Nepal]], [[Sri Lanka]], [[China]], and [[Yemen]].<ref name="Pandit">{{cite journal|date=February 2013|title=Effects of ''Withania somnifera'' on the growth and virulence properties of ''Streptococcus mutans'' and ''Streptococcus sobrinus'' at sub-MIC levels|journal=Anaerobe|volume=19|pages=1–8|doi=10.1016/j.anaerobe.2012.10.007|pmid=23142795|author1=Pandit, S.|author2=Chang, K.-W.|author3=Jeon, J.-G.}}</ref><ref>Hugh Scott & Kenneth Mason, ''Western Arabia and the Red Sea'', Naval Intelligence Division: London 1946, p. 597 {{ISBN|0-7103-1034-X}}.</ref> It prefers dry, stony soil with sun to partial shade. It can be propagated from seeds in the early spring or from [[Cutting (plant)|greenwood cuttings]] in the later spring.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Encyclopedia of herbs & their uses|last=Deni.|first=Bown|date=1995|publisher=RD Press |isbn=0-88850-334-2 |location=Montréal |oclc=32547547}}{{page?|date=March 2025}}</ref>

==Diseases and pests==
''Withania somnifera'' is prone to several pests and diseases. Leaf-spot disease caused by ''[[Alternaria alternata]]'' is the most prevalent disease, which occurs in a severe form in [[Punjab, India|Punjab]], [[Haryana]], and [[Himachal Pradesh]]. Leaf-spot disease reduces the concentration of its [[secondary metabolite]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pati   |first1=P. K. |last2=Sharma |first2=M. |last3=Salar  |first3=R. K. |last4=Sharma |first4=A. |last5=Gupta  |first5=A. P. |last6=Singh  |first6=B. |doi=10.1007/s12088-008-0053-y |title=Studies on leaf spot disease of ''Withania somnifera'' and its impact on secondary metabolites |journal=Indian Journal of Microbiology |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=432–437 |year=2009 |pmid= 23100743|pmc =3476785}}</ref> The leaves are also prone to ''[[Alternaria dianthicola]]'' in India.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maiti |first1=C. K. |last2=Sen |first2=S. |last3=Paul |first3=A. K. |last4=Acharya |first4=K. |date=2007-04-01 |title=First Report of Alternaria dianthicola Causing Leaf Blight on Withania somnifera from India |journal=Plant Disease |volume=91 |issue=4 |page=467 |doi=10.1094/PDIS-91-4-0467B |pmid=30781215 |issn=0191-2917|doi-access=free |bibcode=2007PlDis..91..467M }}</ref>

A [[treehopper]] (''Oxyrachis tarandus'') feeds on the [[apical meristem|apical]] portions of the stem, making them rough and woody in appearance and brown in colour.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sharma |first1=A |last2=Pati |first2=P.K. |title=First report of ''Withania somnifera'' (L.) Dunal, as a New Host of Cowbug (''Oxyrachis tarandus'', Fab.) in plains of Punjab, Northern India. |journal=World Applied Sci. J. |date=2011 |volume=14 |issue=9 |pages=1344–1346}}</ref>

The [[Tetranychus urticae|carmine red spider mite]] (''Tetranychus urticae'') is the most prevalent pest of the plant in India.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Sharma, A. |author2=Pati, P. K. |title=First record of the carmine spider mite, ''Tetranychus urticae'', infesting ''Withania somnifera'' in India |journal=Journal of Insect Science|year=2012 |volume=12 |issue=50 |pages=1–4 |doi=10.1673/031.012.5001 |pmid=22970740 |pmc=3476950}}</ref> In recent years, this plant has been serving as a new reservoir host for an invasive [[mealybug]] species ''[[Phenacoccus solenopsis]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Sharma, A. |author2=Pati, P. K. |title=First record of Ashwagandha as a new host to the invasive mealybug (''Phenacoccus solenopsis'' Tinsley) in India |journal=Entomological News |year=2013 |volume=123 |issue=1 |pages=59–62 |doi=10.3157/021.123.0114 |s2cid=85645762 }}</ref>

==Phytochemistry==
The main [[phytochemistry|phytochemical]] constituents of ''W. somnifera'' are [[withanolide]]s, a group of [[triterpene]] [[lactone]]s that include [[withaferin A]], [[alkaloid]]s, [[steroid]]al [[lactone]]s, [[tropine]], and [[cuscohygrine]].<ref name=drugs/> Forty withanolides, twelve alkaloids, and various sitoindosides have been isolated from this plant species.<ref name=drugs/><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Gómez Afonso |first1=Adrián |last2=Fernandez-Lazaro |first2=Diego |last3=Adams |first3=David P. |last4=Monserdà-Vilaró |first4=Aniol |last5=Fernandez-Lazaro |first5=Cesar I. |date=2023-07-10 |title=Effects of ''Withania somnifera'' (Ashwagandha) on Hematological and Biochemical Markers, Hormonal Behavior, and Oxidant Response in Healthy Adults: A Systematic Review|journal=Current Nutrition Reports |language=en |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=465–477 |doi=10.1007/s13668-023-00481-0 |issn=2161-3311 |pmc=10444651 |pmid=37428341}}</ref> As these withanolides are structurally similar to the [[ginsenoside]]s of ''[[Panax ginseng]]'', ''W. somnifera'' is commonly referred to as "Indian ginseng".<ref name=drugs/>

==Traditional medicine and dietary supplements==
The plant, particularly its root powder, has been used for centuries in [[Ayurveda|traditional Indian medicine]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-03-02 |title=Advice {{!}} Should I take ashwagandha for sleep? Here's what the science says. |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wellness/2024/03/04/should-i-take-ashwagandha-benefits-risks/ |access-date=2024-03-07 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286 |vauthors=Pasricha T}}</ref> ''W. somnifera'' is commonly sold as a [[dietary supplement]] containing root or leaf powder or [[Extract|extracts]].<ref name=drugs/><ref name=NIH/> It is undergoing research for potential effects on stress, anxiety, and sleep, but current [[Evidence-based medicine|clinical evidence]] is insufficient to confirm its safety or efficacy.<ref name=drugs/><ref name=NIH/><ref name="hepa2">{{cite journal |vauthors=Philips CA, Theruvath AH |date=April 2024 |title=A comprehensive review on the hepatotoxicity of herbs used in the Indian (Ayush) systems of alternative medicine |journal=Medicine (Baltimore) |type=Review |volume=103 |issue=16 |article-number=e37903 |doi=10.1097/MD.0000000000037903 |pmc=11029936 |pmid=38640296}}</ref>

===Stress and anxiety===
At oral doses of 300 to 600 mg per day over a three month period, ashwagandha root extract may be useful in treating [[generalized anxiety disorder]], although the evidence for efficacy is tentative and the treatment may cause nausea and diarrhea.<ref name="NIH" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sarris |first=Jerome |last2=Ravindran |first2=Arun |last3=Yatham |first3=Lakshmi N. |last4=Marx |first4=Wolfgang |last5=Rucklidge |first5=Julia J. |last6=McIntyre |first6=Roger S. |last7=Akhondzadeh |first7=Shahin |last8=Benedetti |first8=Francesco |last9=Caneo |first9=Constanza |last10=Cramer |first10=Holger |last11=Cribb |first11=Lachlan |last12=de Manincor |first12=Michael |last13=Dean |first13=Olivia |last14=Deslandes |first14=Andrea Camaz |last15=Freeman |first15=Marlene P. |date=2022 |title=Clinician guidelines for the treatment of psychiatric disorders with nutraceuticals and phytoceuticals: The World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry (WFSBP) and Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments (CANMAT) Taskforce |pmid=35311615 |journal=The World Journal of Biological Psychiatry|volume=23 |issue=6 |pages=424–455 |doi=10.1080/15622975.2021.2013041| issn=1814-1412|url= https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/15622975.2021.2013041}}</ref>

===Sleep===
There is limited evidence that ''W. somnifera'' extract, especially at higher doses and over longer durations, may modestly improve sleep quality and related outcomes, with more noticeable effects in people with [[insomnia]].<ref name=drugs/><ref name=NIH/> A 2021 review concluded that ''W. somnifera'' extract modestly improves sleep quality and quantity in adults, especially those with insomnia, and may reduce anxiety and enhance [[alertness]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cheah |first1=Kae Ling |last2=Norhayati |first2=Mohd Noor |last3=Yaacob |first3=Lili Husniati |last4=Rahman |first4=Razlina Abdul |date=2021-09-24 |title=Effect of Ashwagandha (''Withania somnifera'') extract on sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=16 |issue=9 |article-number=e0257843 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0257843 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=8462692 |pmid=34559859|bibcode=2021PLoSO..1657843C }}</ref>

==Adverse effects==
''Withania somnifera'' may cause [[adverse effect]]s if taken alone or together with [[prescription drug]]s.<ref name=drugs/><ref name="mskcc">{{cite web| title=Ashwagandha |url=https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/ashwagandha|publisher=Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center|access-date=4 April 2024 |date=21 March 2023}}</ref> The most common side effects include [[diarrhea]], headache, [[sedation]], and [[nausea]].<ref name=drugs/><ref name="mskcc"/> Ashwagandha may increase [[testosterone]] levels, which could adversely interact with cancer medications.<ref name=drugs/><ref name=NIH/><ref name=mskcc/>

''Withania somnifera'' can cause [[hepatotoxicity]], and its use as a supplement has been linked to [[herb-induced liver injury]],<ref name=drugs/><ref name="hepa" /> particularly in people with preexisting liver conditions.<ref name="livertox" /> Use of ''W. somnifera'' is not recommended during pregnancy or in people with hormone-sensitive [[prostate cancer]].<ref name=drugs/><ref name="NIH" />
